EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN  

================================================================  
1. Identification Strategy  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Method: Fuzzy Regression-Discontinuity Design (RDD) implemented as a two-stage least squares (2SLS) IV.

Rationale  
• The research question is cross–sectional (“Do large acquirers earn lower announcement returns than small acquirers?”). Simple OLS comparisons are vulnerable to selection: large firms differ systematically in leverage, industry, governance, etc.  
• We need an as-good-as-random shock to firm size that is unrelated to unobserved managerial hubris or deal quality.  
• Annual reconstitution of the Russell 1000/2000 indices provides that shock. On the last trading day in May, FTSE Russell ranks all U.S. firms by market capitalization. Firms just above rank 1,000 enter the Russell 1000 (“large-cap”) and those just below enter the Russell 2000 (“small-cap”). For firms near the cutoff, index assignment is quasi-random because it depends on infinitesimal market-cap differences that managers cannot manipulate.  
• Russell inclusion changes a firm’s shareholder base, analyst coverage, liquidity, and—most important for us—its market-cap and balance-sheet size over the subsequent year (Chen, Noronha & Singal 2004). We therefore use Russell1000 × Post as an instrument for being “large” at the moment the firm announces an acquisition in the following 12 months.  
• Because the probability of being “large” jumps discontinuously at the cutoff but does not change from 0 to 1, we have a fuzzy RD/IV.

================================================================  
2. Treatment and Control  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Running variable: Rank_i,t = firm i’s nationwide rank in market capitalization on the last trading day of May in year t (lower rank = larger firm). Define  
  r_i,t = Rank_i,t – 1,000 (distance from the cutoff).  

Cutoff: r_i,t = 0.  

Treatment indicator (endogenous):  

Large_i,t = 1 if Total Assets_i,t ≥ industry-year 60th percentile (baseline definition used in existing literature) measured immediately before the M&A announcement; 0 otherwise.

Instrument (first stage):  

Z_i,t = 1{Rank_i,t ≤ 1,000} (included in Russell 1000).  

Sample window: |r_i,t| ≤ h where h is a data-driven optimal bandwidth (Imbens–Kalyanaraman or CCT). Only acquisitions announced between July 1 of year t and May 31 of year t+1 (so index status is predetermined).  

Counterfactual: Firms with r_i,t just above 0 (Russell 2000) serve as the control group.

Outcome: CAR[-1,+1]_i,t, the three-day announcement cumulative abnormal return from a standard market-model event study.

================================================================  
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
A1. Continuity of potential outcomes: In the absence of the size shock, expected CARs vary smoothly in r_i,t at the 1,000 cut-off.  
Plausibility: market-cap ranking is mechanical and highly granular; nothing else in the economy changes discontinuously at exactly rank 1,000.  

A2. No precise manipulation of the running variable: Managers cannot fine-tune end-of-May market cap to land on a particular side of the cut-off.  
Plausibility: stock prices are noisy and ownership dispersed; prior studies find no bunching. We will verify with McCrary density test.  

A3. Exclusion restriction (for IV interpretation): Index assignment affects CARs only through its effect on firm size / “large” status, not through other channels.  
Plausibility: Russell inclusion mainly changes liquidity and ownership that mechanically scale the market cap; any remaining direct liquidity effect on returns is second-order over a three-day window. We will test for alternative channels (e.g., contemporaneous volume shocks).  

A4. Stable unit treatment value: One firm’s index status does not affect another’s CAR.  
Reasonable given the narrow window and large number of firms.  

================================================================  
4. Main Threats and Mitigation  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Threat 1: Direct index-membership effects (liquidity, attention) on announcement returns violate exclusion.  
Mitigation: (i) Estimate reduced-form (effect of Z on CAR) and first-stage (effect of Z on size). If reduced-form ÷ first-stage roughly equals OLS coefficient of size on CAR, exclusion likely holds. (ii) Include daily turnover and bid-ask spread controls. (iii) Re-estimate using alternative instruments such as S&P 500 inclusions (placebo).  

Threat 2: Sorting or manipulation around the cutoff.  
Mitigation: McCrary density test; balance tests on pre-determined covariates (Q, leverage, past CARs) within the chosen bandwidth. If imbalance appears, use narrower bandwidth and local linear controls for r_i,t.  

Threat 3: Endogeneity of deal timing relative to reconstitution.  
Mitigation: Require that the announcement occurs at least 30 days after the May ranking date to assure index status is known; run placebo test using announcements in the 30 days before reconstitution (should find no discontinuity).  

================================================================  
5. R Code Outline  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
```r
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 0.  Libraries
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)        # fast fe/iv regressions
library(rdrobust)      # RD estimation
library(ggplot2)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 1.  Load Data  (assumes csv files are in working directory)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
sdc   <- fread("sdc_acquisitions_1980_2001.csv")     # deal-level
crsp  <- fread("crsp_daily_returns.csv")             # daily returns
comp  <- fread("compustat_fundamentals.csv")         # accounting
russ  <- fread("russell_membership.csv")             # rank, index flag

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 2.  Event-study CARs  (–1,+1 market model residuals)
#     **Assume pre-computed and stored in 'car3d'**
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
car  <- fread("acquirer_CARs.csv")                   # firm-day CARs

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 3.  Merge and Variable Construction
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
dt <- merge(sdc, car, by = "deal_id")
dt <- merge(dt, russ[, .(permno, year, rank, russ1000)], 
            by = c("permno", "year"))
dt <- merge(dt, comp[, .(permno, fyear, at, q, leverage, cash_flow)], 
            by.x = c("permno", "year"), by.y = c("permno", "fyear"),
            all.x = TRUE)

# Running variable and instrument
dt[, r := rank - 1000]                 # distance from cutoff
dt[, Z := as.integer(r <= 0)]          # Russell1000 indicator

# Treatment variable: Large if assets ≥ 60th pct. within 2-digit SIC × year
dt[, p60 := quantile(at, .60), by = .(sic2, year)]
dt[, Large := as.integer(at >= p60)]

# Limit to |r| ≤ 300 (initial bandwidth choice)
dt_rdd <- dt[abs(r) <= 300 & announcement_date >= as.Date(paste0(year,"-07-01"))]

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 4.  First-stage and Second-stage (local linear)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Bandwidth selection
bw <- rdbwselect(y = dt_rdd$Large, x = dt_rdd$r)$bws[1]

# 2SLS using fixest
iv_main <- feols(CAR3d ~ 1 | Large ~ Z, data = dt_rdd[abs(r) <= bw],
                 cluster = ~rank)

summary(iv_main)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 5.  Robustness:   (i) Different bandwidth, (ii) Local quadratic
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# (i) Half bandwidth
iv_half <- feols(CAR3d ~ 1 | Large ~ Z, data = dt_rdd[abs(r) <= bw/2],
                 cluster = ~rank)
# (ii) Add running variable controls
iv_quad <- feols(CAR3d ~ poly(r,2,raw=TRUE) | Large ~ Z, 
                 data = dt_rdd[abs(r) <= bw],
                 cluster = ~rank)

etable(list(Main = iv_main, HalfBW = iv_half, Quad = iv_quad),
       tex = FALSE, se.boot = "r")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 6.  Graphical RD check
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
ggplot(dt_rdd, aes(x = r, y = CAR3d)) +
  geom_point(alpha = .4) +
  geom_smooth(data = dt_rdd[r <= 0], method = "lm", se = FALSE,
              formula = y ~ x, color = "blue") +
  geom_smooth(data = dt_rdd[r > 0 ], method = "lm", se = FALSE,
              formula = y ~ x, color = "red") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "RDD of Acquirer CARs at Russell 1000 Cutoff",
       x = "Distance from cutoff (rank – 1000)",
       y = "CAR[-1,+1]")
```

================================================================  
6. Expected Results  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Theory and prior evidence suggest a negative effect of size on announcement returns: larger acquirers earn lower CARs, perhaps due to hubris or weaker monitoring. Existing OLS estimates imply a spread of roughly –2 percentage points between small and large quintiles. After IV correction we expect a somewhat larger (in absolute value) local average treatment effect:  
   LATE(CAR | large vs. small, near cutoff) ≈ –2.5 pp (-0.025).  

Dollar gains—CAR × pre-deal market cap—will remain lower for large firms despite the higher base, implying that the size discount is not just mechanical.

================================================================  
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (RDD)  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
C1. No visible sorting at cutoff (McCrary test)…………… 1  
C2. Covariate continuity within optimal bandwidth……… 1  
C3. Robust to multiple bandwidths and polynomial orders… 1  
C4. Placebo cutoffs (±200 ranks) show no effect………… 0.5  
C5. Results robust when using alternative instruments…… 0.5  
TOTAL = 4 / 5  

================================================================  
The proposed fuzzy RDD leverages a well-validated index-reconstitution shock to generate quasi-random variation in firm size, delivering a credible causal estimate of the “size discount” in M&A announcement returns.
